worksheet.title: Debug Detective
worksheet.subtitle: Find the bug, fix it, explain it
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find a bug in a longer program, fix it, and explain it.

parts.title: You are a debug detective
parts.text: This program is longer, and it has one bug. Run it, find the block that is wrong, fix it, and explain your fix. Then make your own buggy program for a partner to solve. The target is 4.

parts.title: Run it
parts.prompt: Run the program from 0, one block at a time. What number does Bit land on? Did it reach the target (4)?

parts.title: Find and fix the bug
parts.prompt: One block points the WRONG way. Circle it, swap it, and run again. What number does Bit land on now?

parts.title: You try — explain and create
parts.prompt: Explain why your fix worked. Then write your OWN short program with one bug, and the target, for a partner to solve.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: A debug detective runs the code, finds the bug, fixes it, and checks again. You can find wrong, extra, missing, and out-of-order bugs — you are a debugger!

parts.title: Goal
parts.text: The unit finale: students debug a longer program (find the wrong-way block, fix it, explain why the fix works), then create their own buggy program for a partner. Reading and altering code and describing how the change fixes the outcome is C3.2; writing their own program (with a target) is C3.1.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum (Grade 1 — C3 Coding)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.

parts.title: Materials
parts.text: The printed worksheet and a pencil. Optional: a floor number path 0-5 with a marker on 4 so students can run the mystery program and test their own.

parts.title: Run it (about 20-25 min)
text: 1. I DO: run the mystery program — 'start 0, forward 2 to 2, back 1 to 1, forward 1 to 2. Target is 4 — the back 1 sent Bit the wrong way.'
2. WE DO: Exercise 1 — Bit lands on 2. Exercise 2 — circle 'back 1', swap it to 'forward 1'; the program reaches 4 (0 → 2 → 3 → 4).
3. YOU DO: Exercise 3 — students explain the fix (a back block was turning Bit around) and write their own one-bug program with a target.
4. Celebrate: 'You can find and fix every kind of bug — you are a debugger!'

parts.title: Answer key (modelled by the run-gate)
text: Ex 1 — mystery program: 0 → forward 2 → 2 → back 1 → 1 → forward 1 → 2. Bit lands on 2, not the target 4.
Ex 2 — the wrong-way block is 'back 1'; swap it to 'forward 1': 0 → 2 → 3 → 4. Bit reaches the target, 4.

Ex 3 — explanation: the back 1 block moved Bit away from the target; changing it to forward 1 keeps Bit going toward 4. Make-your-own is open; a sample is start 0, forward 1, forward 1 with target 3 (a missing-block bug — add one more forward 1).

parts.title: Watch for & differentiate
text: Common slip: changing more than one block — only one block is wrong; the smallest fix is to swap the back 1.
Simplify: tell students the bug is a wrong-way block and have them find which one.
Extend: have partners trade their make-your-own programs and time how fast they each debug.
Success indicator: the child lands the mystery program on 2, swaps back 1 to forward 1 to reach 4, explains the fix, and writes a solvable one-bug program.
